- `apps/identity-wallet/AppIcon.icon/` -- the layered Icon Composer document for the iOS 26 Liquid Glass icon: `icon.json` (fill gradient + one group: shield.svg over seal.svg, specular on, neutral shadow) + `Assets/*.svg` layers split from `app-icon.svg` with NO baked drop shadows (Liquid Glass supplies lighting/shadow). Referenced in place by the XcodeGen template (`scripts/ios/project.yml`, with a `fileTypes` mapping so the .icon package stays one file); Xcode 26 prefers it over the same-named appiconset, which remains the older-toolchain fallback. Compiled/validated by actool in `just ios-pr-check` (`just _icon-compile`); `just ios-check` verifies the rendered registration. Keep layer geometry in sync with the master SVG when the icon changes
- `src/lib/ipc/` -- Per-domain typed TypeScript wrappers for all Tauri IPC commands, split into `account.ts`, `oauth.ts`, `appearance.ts`, `diagnostics.ts`, `claim.ts`, `identity.ts`, `password-unlock.ts`, `monitor.ts`, `recovery.ts`, `migration.ts`, `handle-change.ts`, `agents.ts`, `app-passwords.ts`, `blob-backup.ts`, `repo-backup.ts`, `notifications.ts`, `self-held-kit.ts` (plus the generic `isCodedError` IPC-error guard in `errors.ts`), all re-exported from `index.ts`; page components import from `$lib/ipc`
- `src-tauri/src/diagnostics.rs` -- in-app, in-memory **network-error breadcrumb log** the user exports from Settings (redacted by construction — operation name, server host, HTTP status, short atproto/transport error code only; never tokens, bodies, handles, or DIDs). A process-global ring buffer (`OnceLock<Mutex<VecDeque>>`, cap 200, unit-of-global like `IdentityStore`) so the deep network seams record without threading a Tauri `State`: `record_server` handles server verdicts, while `record_reqwest_transport` is the shared transport redaction gate (hostname and fixed category only, never the error display or URL path/query). The `export_diagnostics` command renders it to plain text; nothing persists to disk and the user initiates every share, so there is no passive collection to opt out of. **Current capture scope:** server-verdict errors across all `PdsClient` XRPC calls; every `PdsClient` transport failure (`.send()` + body-read); all create-flow `CustosClient` requests (including PAR, token exchange, and health reachability); authenticated `OAuthClient` requests, uploads, lazy refresh, DPoP nonce-refresh retries, and Bearer refresh; plus the monitor's transport case.
- `src/lib/biometric.ts` -- `authenticateBiometric(reason)`: the Face ID / Touch ID (or device-passcode) user-presence gate that precedes irreversible signing IPC calls (sovereign login, agent claim/revoke, migration/did:web submission). A policy gate, not an `invoke()` wrapper — imports the mobile-only `@tauri-apps/plugin-biometric` dynamically and fails closed; tested by `biometric.test.ts`
- `src/lib/unlock.ts` -- `unlockIdentity(did, route?)`: the single place a locked identity is reopened. Asks `getIdentityUnlockRoute` which sign-in the identity's *current* host serves, then runs the biometric `sovereignLogin(did)` or hands a `PasswordUnlockRequest` to the app-level dialog and awaits the user's answer. A policy gate over IPC wrappers rather than an `invoke()` wrapper, so it sits outside `$lib/ipc` alongside `biometric.ts`. The dialog is inverted in (`registerPasswordUnlockPrompt`, returning an unregister for teardown) precisely because `unlockIdentity` is called from the middle of async operations (`catch SESSION_LOCKED → unlock → retry`) that cannot render a form of their own. A dismissed prompt rejects with `UNLOCK_CANCELLED` (`isUnlockCancelled`) — a decision, not a fault, which every screen's `messageFor` maps to `null` so cancelling renders no error. Tested by `unlock.test.ts`
- `src/lib/components/home/PasswordUnlockDialog.svelte` -- the app-level password unlock sheet, mounted once by `+page.svelte` above every step and rendering nothing until `$lib/unlock` needs a password. Names the host, prefills the identifier from the DID document, branches to the emailed two-factor code on `TWO_FACTOR_REQUIRED` (an advance, not an error), and clears every credential it held before it closes
- `src/lib/components/onboarding/` -- one screen component per step of the create / import / recover onboarding flows (the directory listing is the authoritative inventory). The two source-PDS password logins — `PdsAuthScreen` (claim) and `MigrationSourceAuthScreen` (outbound migration) — are thin wrappers over one shared `SourcePasswordAuthScreen` base (form + 2FA branch + shared error switch + styles), each supplying only its copy, IPC fn, and flow-specific error codes
- `src/lib/components/home/` -- the home-surface screen components (the directory listing is the authoritative inventory) plus the DIDAvatar utility component
- `src/lib/deadline.ts` -- PLC recovery deadline utilities (getDeadline, getUrgency, formatCountdown); tested by `deadline.test.ts`
- `src/lib/notification-health.ts` -- the in-app half of the unverified notice: `summarizeNotificationFailures(failures, now)` folds the Notification Service Extension's breadcrumbs into one sentence for Settings — a seven-day window, a **two**-level severity (`quiet`/`info`/`attention`, deliberately NOT the identity urgency ladder, since nothing here can cost an identity), and per-reason wording that answers what happened and whether it is the user's to act on. The worst level in the window wins, and the wording comes from the reason most common AT that level — so one benign post-restart failure never becomes the sentence shown for a week that also holds four key desyncs, and a week of only post-restart failures never manufactures an alarm. Pure and tested by `notification-health.test.ts`
- `src/lib/identity-status.ts` -- the identity screen's status-panel derivation: `deriveIdentityPanelState(changes, deviceKeyUnusable, now)` folds the monitor's answer plus device-key custody into one of the four shared urgency states, `panelLabel(urgency, verified)` is the single label vocabulary the badge and panel share, and `formatCheckedAgo` renders the "checked N ago" line. An active unauthorized change can never produce `safe`, however much recovery window remains — the badge's `safe` means "time left", the panel's means "all clear", which is why the panel derives its state here instead of calling `getUrgency()` on an alert deadline. `verified` reflects `IdentityStatus.checkFailed`: an unreachable directory renders "Not checked" in the calm informational tone, never a green "Secure" the wallet did not verify. Pure and tested by `identity-status.test.ts`
- `src/lib/protection.ts` -- the app-level Defend derivations, shared by the home strip and the Protection surface so the two can never contradict each other: `toRow` lifts one identity into a `ProtectionRow` via `deriveIdentityPanelState` + `isVerified`, `orderRows`/`compareRows` order the list, and `summarize(rows, history, now)` folds every identity into the one statement both surfaces render. Ordering follows the **identity panel's** rule (what is TRUE — critical → expired → warning → safe), deliberately not the home card strips' `activeStrip` rule (what to do NEXT — a dead device key first, because the recovery override the alarm leads to is signed with the key that is missing). That sequencing is not lost: it moves into the summary's copy, which says to recover first when an alarmed wallet also has an unusable key. The worst state always wins the summary, so it can never report "secure" over a row that says otherwise. Also `formatLastVerified`, `describeSweep`, `describeInterval` (reads the cadence from `MonitorHistory.intervalSecs`, never a duplicated literal), `formatClockTime`. Pure and tested by `protection.test.ts`
- `src/lib/alarm-landing.ts` -- the launch/foreground landing decision: `decideAlarmLanding(statuses, dismissed)` answers `none` / `identity` / `protection` from the monitor's latest sweep plus the alarms this app session has already interrupted with, and `alarmKey` identifies an alarm by DID + sorted change CIDs so dismissal survives a foreground without swallowing news. Pure and tested by `alarm-landing.test.ts`; `+page.svelte` owns the in-session dismissal set and the `step === 'home' | 'protection'` guard, so ceremony resumes keep the launch. An expired recovery window still counts as an alarm — it has lost its remedy, not its meaning, and the alarm surface is where that is stated
- `src/lib/identity-cards.ts` -- `loadIdentityCard(did)` / `loadIdentityCards()`: the local facts about a managed identity (cached DID doc + the `docNeedsRotationKeysRefresh` self-heal, handle, PDS, device-key custody, and the `DEVICE_KEY_UNUSABLE` verdict caught as its own state). A composition over `$lib/ipc` rather than an `invoke()` wrapper, so it lives outside the registry alongside `unlock.ts`. Shared by `IdentityListHome` and `ProtectionScreen` because the two must agree — a security surface listing the same identity with different custody answers is the app contradicting itself. An identity whose read fails becomes a degraded card, never a dropped one, and carries **`degraded: true`**: its other fields are then placeholders indistinguishable from a healthy identity's (`deviceKeyUnusable: false` is exactly what a good key produces), so without the flag `toRow` would derive `safe` and `summarize` would fold an identity the wallet never managed to read into "All identities secure". `degraded` resolves to `verified: false` — overriding even the did:web verified-by-construction rule, which says a domain-anchored identity needs no directory sweep, not that one we failed to load is fine
- `src/routes/+page.svelte` -- Three-flow state machine starting at add_identity (AddIdentityScreen, the situation question; its "my server is gone" answer opens the `server_gone` routing screen, which points at an existing identity's move_or_rebuild door or chains into recover_start); Create flow: add_identity -> identity_method (did:plc / did:web fork) -> [did:plc: pds_config; new did:web: did_web_path -> did_web_domain -> pds_config] -> ... -> did_ceremony (did:web: did_web_ceremony) -> ... -> home; Import flow: add_identity -> identity_input -> pds_auth -> email_verification -> review_operation -> claim_success -> home (existing did:web forks at identity_method -> did_web_path -> did_web_existing -> importDidWebIdentity -> migration_start); Recover flow: add_identity -> recover_start -> recover_shares -> [recover_escrow] -> recover_verify -> recover_epilogue -> recover_backup (ShamirBackupScreen reuse, `confirmRecoveryBackup` teardown) -> recover_success -> home, with a launch-time resume hook (`getPendingRecoveryEpilogue()` on mount routes straight to recover_epilogue when a rotation epilogue was interrupted); Home: home (IdentityListHome) -> identity_detail (IdentityScreen, the instrument panel) -> { move_or_rebuild | manage_identity -> advanced_tools | app_passwords | my_agents | oauth_consent_approval | alert_detail -> recovery_override }, plus home -> settings (SettingsScreen: appearance, background media backup, the notification-health readout, diagnostics export); visibilitychange handler calls checkIdentityStatus() on foreground and lands on the alarm surface via `$lib/alarm-landing` when one is live and unshown
- `src/routes/+layout.ts` -- `ssr = false; prerender = false` (global SPA config)
- `svelte.config.js` -- adapter-static with `pages: 'dist'` (SPA mode, matches tauri.conf.json)
- `vite.config.ts` -- Tauri-compatible Vite server (clearScreen, HMR via TAURI_DEV_HOST, envPrefix)

## Troubleshooting

### `cargo tauri ios dev` fails with "Connection refused"

You launched the Xcode build manually (clicking Run in Xcode) instead of through `cargo tauri ios dev`. Xcode's "Build Rust Code" phase calls `cargo tauri ios xcode-script`, which connects back to the `cargo tauri ios dev` process via JSON-RPC. There is no server to connect to if the build was not initiated by `cargo tauri ios dev`.

**Fix:** Always use `cargo tauri ios dev` from the terminal. Do not click Run in Xcode.

---

### `error: can't find crate for 'core'` — `aarch64-apple-ios-sim` target not installed

The Nix `rust-default` package (used by `languages.rust` in devenv) does not ship iOS cross-compilation stdlibs. This was the historical state of the project before the rustup migration.

**Fix:** Already resolved. `devenv.nix` uses `pkgs.rustup` with project-local `RUSTUP_HOME`/`CARGO_HOME`. On first `nix develop`, `enterShell` runs `rustup toolchain install` which reads `rust-toolchain.toml` and installs `aarch64-apple-ios-sim` stdlib automatically.

If you see this after a fresh clone: make sure you entered the dev shell from the **workspace root** (not from `apps/identity-wallet/`) so that `CARGO_HOME` resolves correctly.

---

### `error: tool 'simctl' not found` or `xcrun simctl list` fails

The Nix devenv's Darwin setup hooks override `DEVELOPER_DIR` (and `SDKROOT`) to a Nix apple-sdk stub that has no runtime tools. The `xcbuild` xcrun shim in PATH delegates to `$DEVELOPER_DIR/usr/bin/xcrun` — if `DEVELOPER_DIR` points at a Nix stub, it fails.

**Fix:** Already resolved automatically. `devenv.nix`'s `enterShell` sources `apps/identity-wallet/scripts/ios-env.sh`. The catch: `/usr/bin/xcode-select -p` and `/usr/bin/xcrun` both **honor `DEVELOPER_DIR` above the system Xcode selection**, so calling them by absolute path is not enough — they echo the Nix stub straight back. `ios-env.sh` first **unsets `DEVELOPER_DIR` when it points into `/nix/store`**, so `xcode-select -p` falls through to the real Xcode selection; it then re-exports `DEVELOPER_DIR` to that real path. (A genuine Xcode-provided `DEVELOPER_DIR` — not under `/nix/store` — is left untouched, so the Xcode Run Script keeps Xcode's own value.)

If you still see this: verify with `echo $DEVELOPER_DIR` inside the dev shell. If it shows a Nix store path, exit and re-enter the shell from the workspace root.

---

### `sandbox-exec: sandbox_apply: Operation not permitted` (Tauri ios-api build)

Swift Package Manager sandboxes its manifest compilation using `sandbox-exec`. On macOS 26 (Tahoe), `sandbox_apply()` returns `EPERM` in this context, causing `swift-rs`'s build script (used by Tauri) to fail with "Failed to compile swift package Tauri".

**Fix:** Already resolved and applied automatically. A local patch of `swift-rs` 1.0.7 at `apps/identity-wallet/swift-rs-patch/` adds `--disable-sandbox` to the `swift build` invocation inside `SwiftLinker::link`. The workspace `Cargo.toml` wires this in via `[patch.crates-io]`. See `docs/ios-upstream-bugs.md` for details. Remove the patch entry when swift-rs ships a fix upstream.

---

### `Failed to update the excludes stack to see if a path is excluded` (Xcode user script sandbox)

Xcode 14+ enables `ENABLE_USER_SCRIPT_SANDBOXING=YES` by default in generated projects, wrapping Run Script build phases in `sandbox-exec`. On macOS 26 (Tahoe), this sandbox blocks Cargo's `readdir()` calls during package fingerprinting, producing:

```
error: failed to determine package fingerprint for build script for identity-wallet v0.1.0
Caused by: Failed to update the excludes stack to see if a path is excluded
```

**Fix:** Already resolved automatically. The `scripts/ios/project.yml` template sets `ENABLE_USER_SCRIPT_SANDBOXING: NO`, which every `cargo tauri ios init` renders into the generated project; `just ios-check` verifies the setting is in place.

---

### `Undefined symbols ... _SC*` / `_ASWebAuthenticationSession*` — an Apple framework not linked at `Ld`

The Rust code compiles, then Xcode's link step fails with `Undefined symbols for architecture arm64:` naming Apple framework symbols — e.g. `_SCDynamicStore...` / `_SCNetworkReachability...` (Apple's `SystemConfiguration.framework`, which the `system-configuration` crate needs — pulled in transitively by `hickory-resolver` for system DNS config and `reqwest` for system proxy detection), or `_ASWebAuthenticationSessionErrorDomain` (Apple's `AuthenticationServices.framework`, which the vendored `tauri-plugin-auth-session` needs via `objc2-authentication-services` / `ASWebAuthenticationSession`).

Host builds (`cargo test` / `cargo build`) link fine because **rustc** does the final link and honors the crate's `#[link(name = "...", kind = "framework")]`. On iOS the crate is built as a `staticlib` (`libapp.a`) and **Xcode** does the final link — it never sees that embedded directive, so the framework must be declared in the Xcode project or the symbols stay undefined. A `build.rs` `cargo:rustc-link-lib=framework=...` does NOT help (same staticlib → Xcode gap).

**Fix:** Already resolved automatically. The `scripts/ios/project.yml` template renders `OTHER_LDFLAGS = "$(inherited) -framework SystemConfiguration -framework AuthenticationServices"` from `bundle > iOS > frameworks` in `tauri.conf.json` (the same list also produces xcodegen `sdk:` link dependencies), and `just ios-check` verifies every listed framework. The historical footgun this design removes: `bundle.iOS.frameworks` used to seed only a FRESH project.yml, because `cargo tauri ios init` preserves an existing one — with the custom template, project.yml is re-rendered from config on every init, so the config is now the enforced mechanism. To link another Apple framework a new Rust dep requires, **add it to `bundle > iOS > frameworks` in `tauri.conf.json`** and re-run `cargo tauri ios init` + `just ios-postinit` — never hand-edit `OTHER_LDFLAGS` in the generated project (a second `OTHER_LDFLAGS` assignment for the same build config shadows, not appends to, the first, silently dropping a framework — `just ios-check` detects that state).

---

### `libapp.a ... is not permitted` / `Invalid bundle structure` on TestFlight upload

`cargo tauri ios build` succeeds and `xcrun altool` then rejects the upload (HTTP 409): *"The 'Obsign.app/libapp.a' binary file is not permitted. Your app cannot contain standalone executables or libraries."* (tauri#13578.)

cargo-mobile2 lists the `Externals` directory (which holds the Rust staticlib `libapp.a`) as a project source with **no explicit `buildPhase`**, so XcodeGen infers `resources` and copies the raw `.a` into the `.app` — which App Store validation forbids. The library is also (correctly) **linked** via the separate `framework: libapp.a` entry + `LIBRARY_SEARCH_PATHS`, so excluding it from resources is safe.

**Fix:** Already resolved automatically. The `scripts/ios/project.yml` template sets `Externals → buildPhase: none`, so xcodegen never emits a `libapp.a in Resources` entry (the `framework: libapp.a` link dependency is kept). `just ios-check` verifies both layers.

---

### `base64: invalid option -- 'o'` during `cargo tauri ios build` signing

The build reads `IOS_CERTIFICATE` and fails decoding it: `base64: invalid option -- 'o'`. In the Nix dev shell, GNU coreutils `base64` shadows macOS's BSD `base64` in `PATH`, but Tauri's cert decode uses BSD-only flags (`-i`/`-o`). (CI is unaffected — the runner has no Nix.)

**Fix:** Already resolved automatically. `scripts/ios-env.sh` (under `EZPDS_IOS_BUILD=1`) shims `/usr/bin/base64` ahead of the Nix one via a tiny symlink dir on `PATH` — surgical (only `base64`), leaving every other Nix tool untouched.

1	// The Notification Service Extension: the only place a sealed push is ever plaintext.
2	//
3	// A Custos instance HPKE-seals a notification to this device's key and hands it to a relay
4	// that holds the APNs key but no decryption key. The relay and Apple both carry the payload
5	// as opaque bytes beside a placeholder alert ("Custos / Encrypted notification"), and
6	// `mutable-content: 1` routes it here for the ~30 seconds iOS allows before it gives up and
7	// shows the placeholder.
8	//
9	// # The constraint that shapes everything below
10	//
11	// **An NSE cannot suppress an alert push.** If this code fails, times out, or declines to
12	// attach content, iOS displays the original payload anyway. So "drop what we cannot verify"
13	// is not on the menu; the only thing under this extension's control is *what the user reads*.
14	// The rule is therefore absolute: content that opened under HPKE Auth mode renders as
15	// content, and everything else renders as the explicit unverified notice. Never a guess,
16	// never a partial render, never the placeholder passed through as though it were news.
17	//
18	// That is what keeps a relay's junk push from being an impersonation. The relay can always
19	// generate noise — it holds the APNs key — but noise arrives labelled as unverifiable, which
20	// is detectable spam and grounds for switching relays, not a forged message from your server.
21	
22	import UserNotifications
23	
24	/// The decision the extension makes about one payload, split out from the `UNNotification`
25	/// machinery so every branch is reachable from a test.
26	enum NotifyOutcome: Equatable {
27	    case rendered(NotifyPayload)
28	    case unverified(NotifyFailureReason, kid: Int?)
29	}
30	
31	enum NotifyResolver {
32	    /// The user-visible copy for a payload this device cannot vouch for.
33	    ///
34	    /// Deliberately says what happened and nothing more. It names no sender ("from your
35	    /// Custos instance" is a category, not a claim about which one), states no cause the
36	    /// extension cannot know, and offers no action — the actionable version of this lives in
37	    /// Settings, where the breadcrumbs can say whether it happened once or twenty times.
38	    static let unverifiedTitle = "Unverified notification"
39	    static let unverifiedBody = "Couldn't verify a notification from your Custos instance."
40	
41	    /// Resolve an APNs `userInfo` into what should be shown.
42	    ///
43	    /// Pure over its inputs — the Keychain reads happen in the caller — so the whole failure
44	    /// ladder is exercisable on a simulator with no push and no registered key.
45	    static func resolve(
46	        userInfo: [AnyHashable: Any],
47	        recipientPrivateKey: Data?,
48	        pins: PinnedSenderKeys
49	    ) -> NotifyOutcome {
50	        guard let envelope = NotifyEnvelope.parse(userInfo: userInfo) else {
51	            return .unverified(.malformedPayload, kid: nil)
52	        }
53	        guard let recipientPrivateKey else {
54	            return .unverified(.keysUnavailable, kid: envelope.kid)
55	        }
56	
57	        let candidates = pins.candidates(for: envelope.kid)
58	        guard !candidates.isEmpty else {
59	            return .unverified(.unknownKid, kid: envelope.kid)
60	        }
61	
62	        // Try every key pinned under this `kid`. See `PinnedSenderKeys.candidates` for why
63	        // there can be more than one; Auth mode makes a wrong guess free.
64	        for didKey in candidates {
65	            guard let senderBytes = DidKey.p256PublicKeyBytes(from: didKey) else { continue }
66	            guard let plaintext = NotifyCrypto.open(
67	                recipientPrivateKey: recipientPrivateKey,
68	                senderPublicKey: senderBytes,
69	                encapsulatedKey: envelope.enc,
70	                ciphertext: envelope.ct
71	            ) else { continue }
72	
73	            // Past this point the payload is authenticated: only a holder of a pinned sender
74	            // private key could have produced it. A body we cannot parse is therefore our own
75	            // bug or a version skew, not an attack — but it still cannot be rendered as
76	            // content, because there is no content to render.
77	            guard let payload = NotifyPayload.decode(plaintext) else {
78	                return .unverified(.malformedPlaintext, kid: envelope.kid)
79	            }
80	            return .rendered(payload)
81	        }
82	
83	        return .unverified(.openFailed, kid: envelope.kid)
84	    }
85	}
86	
87	final class NotificationService: UNNotificationServiceExtension {
88	    private var contentHandler: ((UNNotificationContent) -> Void)?
89	    private var bestAttempt: UNMutableNotificationContent?
90	
91	    override func didReceive(
92	        _ request: UNNotificationRequest,
93	        withContentHandler contentHandler: @escaping (UNNotificationContent) -> Void
94	    ) {
95	        self.contentHandler = contentHandler
96	        guard let content = request.content.mutableCopy() as? UNMutableNotificationContent else {
97	            // `UNNotificationContent.mutableCopy()` is documented to return the mutable class, so
98	            // this is a platform-contract violation rather than a state a payload can produce.
99	            // It still cannot be allowed to deliver `request.content`: that content is immutable,
100	            // so the sealed block cannot be stripped from it, and its title/body are the relay's
101	            // placeholder — the one combination the extension's rule forbids. A fresh content
102	            // carrying only the notice is the sole way to honour both halves here.
103	            //
104	            // No breadcrumb: the failure vocabulary describes payloads, and reporting this as a
105	            // payload problem would send the user looking at their keys for a bug in ours.
106	            contentHandler(Self.unverifiedContent())
107	            return
108	        }
109	        bestAttempt = content
110	
111	        let outcome = NotifyResolver.resolve(
112	            userInfo: request.content.userInfo,
113	            recipientPrivateKey: NotifyKeychain.read(
114	                account: NotifyKeychain.notificationKeyAccount
115	            ),
116	            pins: PinnedSenderKeys.parse(
117	                NotifyKeychain.read(account: NotifyKeychain.pinnedSenderKeysAccount)
118	            )
119	        )
120	
121	        switch outcome {
122	        case let .rendered(payload):
123	            content.title = payload.title
124	            content.body = payload.body
125	        case let .unverified(reason, kid):
126	            content.title = NotifyResolver.unverifiedTitle
127	            content.body = NotifyResolver.unverifiedBody
128	            NotifyBreadcrumbs.record(reason, kid: kid)
129	        }
130	
131	        Self.finish(content)
132	        contentHandler(content)
133	    }
134	
135	    /// iOS is about to give up on us.
136	    ///
137	    /// Whatever is in `bestAttempt` is delivered, so this path has to satisfy the same two
138	    /// obligations `didReceive` does — say "unverified" rather than let the relay's placeholder
139	    /// stand in for the server's words, and strip the sealed block. Neither gets an exception
140	    /// for running late: a timeout is the one route by which unstripped ciphertext, under a
141	    /// title the user reads as authentic, could reach the delivered-notification list.
142	    override func serviceExtensionTimeWillExpire() {
143	        guard let contentHandler, let bestAttempt else { return }
144	        // The presence of the sealed block IS the "we never finished" signal — `finish` strips it
145	        // and writes the notice in the same breath, so it can only still be here if resolution
146	        // was cut short. Testing that rather than the title keeps the two facts from drifting.
147	        if bestAttempt.userInfo[NotifyEnvelope.userInfoKey] != nil {
148	            bestAttempt.title = NotifyResolver.unverifiedTitle
149	            bestAttempt.body = NotifyResolver.unverifiedBody
150	        }
151	        Self.finish(bestAttempt)
152	        contentHandler(bestAttempt)
153	    }
154	
155	    /// The last thing done to any content that leaves this extension.
156	    ///
157	    /// The sealed block has served its purpose and must not ride along into the delivered
158	    /// notification, where the app — and anything reading `UNUserNotificationCenter`'s delivered
159	    /// list — would see ciphertext it has no use for. Factored out because "every exit path"
160	    /// is the actual requirement, and inlining it at each one is how an exit path gets missed.
161	    private static func finish(_ content: UNMutableNotificationContent) {
162	        content.userInfo.removeValue(forKey: NotifyEnvelope.userInfoKey)
163	    }
164	
165	    /// A fresh content carrying nothing but the unverified notice.
166	    ///
167	    /// For the exit where no mutable copy exists to strip, so substituting content is the only
168	    /// way to avoid delivering the sealed block.
169	    private static func unverifiedContent() -> UNMutableNotificationContent {
170	        let content = UNMutableNotificationContent()
171	        content.title = NotifyResolver.unverifiedTitle
172	        content.body = NotifyResolver.unverifiedBody
173	        return content
174	    }
175	}

1	// The pure half of the Notification Service Extension: everything that turns bytes into
2	// other bytes, with no Keychain, no CryptoKit, and no UserNotifications.
3	//
4	// It lives apart from NotificationService.swift for the same reason the wallet's Rust keeps
5	// `_impl` cores away from Tauri commands — this is the part an XCTest can drive on a
6	// simulator, and the part the Rust↔CryptoKit fixture cross-check exercises.
7	
8	import Foundation
9	
10	/// The `ezpds` object a sealed push carries beside its placeholder `aps` alert.
11	///
12	/// Wire shape (see `crates/notify-relay/src/protocol.rs`):
13	/// `{ "v": 1, "kid": 3, "enc": "<b64url>", "ct": "<b64url>" }`
14	struct NotifyEnvelope: Equatable {
15	    /// Protocol version. Only `1` is understood; anything else is a payload sealed by a
16	    /// newer instance for a newer extension, and must render as unverified rather than be
17	    /// guessed at.
18	    static let supportedVersion = 1
19	
20	    /// The `userInfo` key the sealed block travels under. Named once because it is used for two
21	    /// opposite purposes — reading the envelope, and *removing* it before delivery — and a typo
22	    /// in the second would leak ciphertext into the delivered-notification list silently.
23	    static let userInfoKey = "ezpds"
24	
25	    let version: Int
26	    /// The instance-scoped sender-key id. Not a global identifier: two Custos instances both
27	    /// start their `kid` sequence at 1, which is why the pin store is keyed by host and every
28	    /// candidate under this id is tried.
29	    let kid: Int
30	    /// HPKE encapsulated key — 65 raw bytes for DHKEM(P-256).
31	    let enc: Data
32	    /// AEAD ciphertext with the 16-byte AES-GCM tag appended.
33	    let ct: Data
34	
35	    /// Read the envelope out of an APNs `userInfo` dictionary.
36	    ///
37	    /// Returns `nil` for anything that is not a well-formed v1 envelope — a junk push from a
38	    /// misbehaving relay, a `content-available` ping, or a future version. The caller renders
39	    /// all of those identically (the unverified notice), so this deliberately does not
40	    /// distinguish "absent" from "malformed": neither is content this device can vouch for.
41	    static func parse(userInfo: [AnyHashable: Any]) -> NotifyEnvelope? {
42	        guard let block = userInfo[userInfoKey] as? [String: Any],
43	              let version = block["v"] as? Int,
44	              version == supportedVersion,
45	              let kid = block["kid"] as? Int,
46	              let encText = block["enc"] as? String,
47	              let ctText = block["ct"] as? String,
48	              let enc = Data(base64URLEncoded: encText),
49	              let ct = Data(base64URLEncoded: ctText),
50	              !enc.isEmpty, !ct.isEmpty
51	        else { return nil }
52	
53	        return NotifyEnvelope(version: version, kid: kid, enc: enc, ct: ct)
54	    }
55	}
56	
57	/// The decrypted plaintext a Custos instance seals.
58	///
59	/// Wire shape: `{ "type": …, "title": …, "body": …, "data": { … }, "pad": "…" }`. `pad` is
60	/// dropped on the floor here — its whole job was to make the *serialized APNs request* land
61	/// on a padding bucket, which is finished by the time these bytes exist.
62	struct NotifyPayload: Equatable, Decodable {
63	    let type: String
64	    let title: String
65	    let body: String
66	
67	    /// Decode sealed plaintext, rejecting a payload with nothing to render.
68	    ///
69	    /// An empty title *and* body would produce a banner indistinguishable from a silent
70	    /// delivery failure, so it is treated as a malformed payload and rendered as the
71	    /// unverified notice instead — the extension's one rule is that it never shows something
72	    /// it cannot stand behind.
73	    static func decode(_ plaintext: Data) -> NotifyPayload? {
74	        guard let payload = try? JSONDecoder().decode(NotifyPayload.self, from: plaintext),
75	              !(payload.title.isEmpty && payload.body.isEmpty)
76	        else { return nil }
77	        return payload
78	    }
79	}
80	
81	// MARK: - base64url
82	
83	extension Data {
84	    /// Decode unpadded base64url — the encoding every binary field in the envelope uses
85	    /// (`URL_SAFE_NO_PAD` on the Rust side). Foundation only speaks standard base64 with
86	    /// padding, so translate the alphabet and re-pad.
87	    init?(base64URLEncoded input: String) {
88	        var text = input.replacingOccurrences(of: "-", with: "+")
89	            .replacingOccurrences(of: "_", with: "/")
90	        let remainder = text.count % 4
91	        if remainder == 1 {
92	            // 4n+1 is not a length any base64 encoding can produce; padding it would
93	            // manufacture a decodable string out of corrupt input.
94	            return nil
95	        }
96	        if remainder > 0 {
97	            text += String(repeating: "=", count: 4 - remainder)
98	        }
99	        guard let decoded = Data(base64Encoded: text) else { return nil }
100	        self = decoded
101	    }
102	}
103	
104	// MARK: - did:key
105	
106	/// Decode a P-256 `did:key` into its raw SEC1 public-key bytes.
107	///
108	/// The pinned sender keys arrive from Custos as `did:key:z…` strings and are stored verbatim
109	/// by the wallet (`notifications.rs`), so the extension has to undo the encoding itself:
110	/// multibase base58btc (`z` prefix) wrapping the multicodec varint `0x1200` — written
111	/// little-endian-base128 as `0x80 0x24` — followed by a 33-byte compressed point.
112	///
113	/// Returns `nil` for anything that is not exactly that. A sender key this device cannot
114	/// decode is simply not a candidate; HPKE Auth mode would fail closed on it anyway, so
115	/// skipping costs nothing and misreading could not gain anything.
116	enum DidKey {
117	    /// The multicodec prefix for `p256-pub`, varint-encoded.
118	    static let p256Prefix: [UInt8] = [0x80, 0x24]
119	    /// A compressed SEC1 P-256 point: 1 tag byte + 32-byte X.
120	    static let compressedPointLength = 33
121	
122	    static func p256PublicKeyBytes(from didKey: String) -> Data? {
123	        guard didKey.hasPrefix("did:key:z") else { return nil }
124	        let multibase = String(didKey.dropFirst("did:key:z".count))
125	        guard let decoded = Base58.decode(multibase),
126	              decoded.count == p256Prefix.count + compressedPointLength,
127	              Array(decoded.prefix(p256Prefix.count)) == p256Prefix
128	        else { return nil }
129	        return Data(decoded.dropFirst(p256Prefix.count))
130	    }
131	}
132	
133	/// base58btc, the one multibase alphabet `did:key` uses.
134	///
135	/// Hand-rolled because the extension links nothing but system frameworks: a Swift package
136	/// dependency in an NSE is a second supply chain in the one target that runs on a locked
137	/// screen, for ~30 lines of long division.
138	enum Base58 {
139	    private static let alphabet = Array("REDACTED".utf8)
140	
141	    static func decode(_ input: String) -> [UInt8]? {
142	        var bytes: [UInt8] = [0]
143	        for character in input.utf8 {
144	            guard let value = alphabet.firstIndex(of: character) else { return nil }
145	            var carry = value
146	            for index in bytes.indices.reversed() {
147	                carry += 58 * Int(bytes[index])
148	                bytes[index] = UInt8(carry & 0xff)
149	                carry >>= 8
150	            }
151	            while carry > 0 {
152	                bytes.insert(UInt8(carry & 0xff), at: 0)
153	                carry >>= 8
154	            }
155	        }
156	        // Every leading '1' encodes one leading zero byte, which the arithmetic above cannot
157	        // recover (it carries no magnitude).
158	        var leadingZeros = 0
159	        for character in input.utf8 {
160	            guard character == alphabet[0] else { break }
161	            leadingZeros += 1
162	        }
163	        // Drop the seed byte and any zeros the long division introduced, then restore the
164	        // encoded ones.
165	        let significant = Array(bytes.drop(while: { $0 == 0 }))
166	        return Array(repeating: 0, count: leadingZeros) + significant
167	    }
168	}

I've got the full picture now. I'm adding two columns to the pending OAuth authorizations table—a match_code field and a push_dispatched_at timestamp—where a null match_code indicates no push has been sent yet and no number matching is needed.

Now I'm updating the notify_device function to return the count of devices enqueued, and I need to handle that return value at the call site in agent_claim. I'm also adding match_code as an optional field to the PendingOAuthAuthorization struct and updating the database queries to select and map it. The set_push_dispatched function will update the authorization record to set both the match_code and timestamp, but only if the status is still pending and match_code hasn't been set yet. Finally, I'm creating a helper function in oauth_authorize.rs that dispatches the login approval push after inserting the pending authorization and recording the audit event.

Resolving the login_hint locally by checking if it's a DID or normalizing it as a handle, then looking it up in the database without any outbound resolution. I'll verify an active local account exists, generate a two-digit match code, and send a push notification with the request details and a message asking the user to approve the sign-in attempt.

If the push notification is successfully enqueued, I'll mark it as dispatched in the database, log an audit event with the device count, and return the match code to display on the page. If anything fails, the page renders without a number as a clean fallback. I'm also refactoring `create_pending_request` to return a struct that includes the optional match code, and updating the wallet consent template to display a "push sent" message when the code is present.

Now I'm adding the match code to the consent request data structures and updating the approval flow to handle it. The match number displays prominently above the QR code as the primary path when a push is dispatched, with the QR code serving as a fallback. I'm adding a `match_required` flag to track whether a match code exists, and updating the approval handler to validate the match code when the user approves.

For the validation logic, if a match code is required and the submitted code doesn't match, I return a distinct 401 error with a specific message so the wallet can distinguish it from other auth failures. This allows retries since the request doesn't transition to a terminal state. Denials skip the check entirely since declining is the safe action. I'm keeping the comparison simple with a basic equality check rather than constant-time comparison, since we're only dealing with two digits and rate limiting handles abuse.

I'm now thinking through how to map this error distinctly in the wallet's confirmation flow, since 401 currently maps to ApprovalRejected but I need to differentiate a match code failure from a general rejection. The wallet already knows from the preview whether a match is required, so it can prompt the user to enter the two digits and send them along. If they enter the wrong number, the server returns a 401 with a distinguishable error body. I need to check what ErrorCode variants are available and how ApiError serializes them — if the body includes a code field like `{"error": "AuthenticationRequired", "message": "..."}`, the wallet can match on that. Otherwise I might need to match on the message text itself, which feels fragile. Better approach: use a 403 Forbidden for a match mismatch specifically, keeping 401 for signature failures, so the wallet can distinguish them by status code alone. Checking whether exposing the mismatch versus rejection distinction creates an oracle problem — but since the check runs after signature and authority verification, only the genuine key-holder can see it, so it's safe. Now I need to add a `PushDispatched` audit event variant and verify the V056 migration has a CHECK constraint on the event_type column for oauth_consent_audit_events; if it does, V060 will need to handle rebuilding that constraint when introducing the new event type.

Rate limiting on match-code guessing through approve is already bounded by the consent_action limiter (30 requests per 5 minutes per IP) plus the signature requirement. I'll update the Bruno API documentation files to clarify the matchCode field and matchRequired response field, then add test cases to verify that approving without a matchCode still returns 403.

For the oauth_consent.rs tests, I need to seed pending requests with a match_code and verify the full flow: missing code returns 403, wrong code returns 403, correct code returns 200. I'll also test that denial doesn't require the match number and that the preview correctly includes the matchRequired flag.

For oauth_authorize.rs, the login_hint dispatch test is tricky because the test harness doesn't have a live notify infrastructure, so I'll extract the hint-to-DID resolution logic into a separate testable helper function and unit-test that independently, then use the notify_e2e_test harness for the full integration path. Relay enqueue just means the message is sealed and queued, not necessarily delivered — if the queue worker fails later, the match code is still required and the number stays on the page, which is fine. The `notify_device` call receives state through `&AppState` inside `create_pending_request`, so that works. One thing to note: requiring the match code also blocks old-wallet approvals on push-dispatched requests, which only happens when login_hint matches a local account with registered devices and notify is configured — that's acceptable.

For the iOS notification service, I'm adding a `RouteData` struct to `NotifyPayload` with optional `requestId` and `did` fields that decode tolerantly. In the `.rendered` branch, when the payload type is "login-approval", the route info needs to survive...

I'm injecting route data into the user info dictionary under the key "ezpdsRoute" with the type, requestId, and did — keeping this deliberate for now by scoping to "login-approval" only, though the structure could support other routable types later. The `finish()` method strips the "ezpds" key, so the injection happens after that, and the timeWillExpire path intentionally never injects since it's unverified. Tests for NotifyResolverTests will verify that payloads with data decode correctly.

For testability, I'm extracting the route logic into a pure helper function — either `NotifyRoute.from(payload)` or a static method like `routeUserInfo(for:)` in NotifyEnvelope.swift — so it can be tested independently without relying on the hard-to-test didReceive callback. I'll also update ios/AGENTS.md to document this.

On the Rust side for APNS, I need to add a delegate method to handle notification taps, which requires a UNUserNotificationCenterDelegate. Since objc2 lets me define classes at runtime, I can create a minimal delegate object to wire this up.

Adding the notification response handler... The method signature takes the notification center, response object, and a completion handler block. I need to extract the userInfo dictionary from the notification response, pull out the "ezpdsRoute" data containing type, requestId, and did fields, then store this as a pending route in a static mutex and fire off a Tauri event with the route information. The completion block needs to be called once I'm done processing.

I could keep this simpler by parsing the userInfo dictionary in Rust using the objc2_foundation API rather than doing all the extraction in the handler itself. Then I'd set up a portable core module with a struct holding the route kind, request ID, and DID, backed by a global OnceLock wrapping a mutex. This gives me helper functions to store and retrieve pending routes, plus a Tauri command that the frontend can call to check if a notification route is waiting.

For the iOS side, the APNS handler would store the route and emit an event that the frontend listens for on warm start. On the wallet side, I need to update the consent preview to include a match_required boolean that deserializes from the server's camelCase matchRequired field with a default of false for older servers, then add a match_code parameter to the confirm command and the approval request struct.

The key is using skip_serializing_if to only send match_code when it's Some, so older servers with deny_unknown_fields won't reject it. For the error mapping, I should change 403 responses to a new MatchCodeMismatch error instead of the current ApprovalRejected, since old servers don't return 403 on this endpoint anyway.

Now I'm adding tests to verify the match code gets sent in the request body and that 403 properly maps to the new error. On the TypeScript side, I'm updating the IPC layer to include matchRequired as a boolean on ConsentPreview and adding an optional matchCode parameter to confirmOAuthConsent, plus a new MATCH_CODE_MISMATCH error type. In the UI, I'm adding an initialRequestId prop that triggers a loading state and fetches the preview, then in the review phase if matchRequired is true, I'll show a number entry field for the two-digit code.

The field stays disabled until it matches the pattern, and on approval it passes the code to confirmOAuthConsent; if there's a mismatch error, the field shows an error message and clears. For the page routing, I'm deciding where notification-triggered flows should land in the precedence order — after removals and recovery epilogue but before alarm takeover, since an explicit notification tap should take priority over background alarms. I need to load the DID document in the consent approval step by checking how identity_detail handles it, then set up a warm listener for notification routes. For the harness, I'll add registry handlers for the pending notification route and update the consent fakes to support matchRequired: false, possibly with a scenario to exercise the match UI through the preview function.

For testing the match UI, I could make the fake return matchRequired based on the user code input — something like checking if the code starts with "PUSH" to toggle it on. This is stateless and deterministic, so it's acceptable. I'll also need to update the docs-generate command for the IPC reference with the new take_pending_notification_route and changed signatures, decide on a number format (2-digit style like GitHub), and update the design plan Phase C section with a "Landed" note plus the relevant AGENTS.md files.

Now I'm tracking the database schema updates — the oauth_consent table needs a match-code mention, and I'll need a V060 migration entry in db/AGENTS.md. For the changelog, I need to check the existing convention for fragment naming and whether MM refs are allowed, then create an entry following that pattern. The implementation order is server first, then NSE, wallet, and finally docs/checks.

For the environment setup, I'll use the main checkout's devenv with the --manifest-path flag pointing to the ezpds directory, and run rustfmt directly on touched files. Let me start by verifying the V056 SQL CHECK constraint, reviewing the common ErrorCode variants, and wiring up the rate_limit consent_action logic.
I have the full picture now. I'll pin down the audit-table CHECK constraint and available error codes, then start implementing.

content.thinking:
I need to update the oauth_authorize.rs file with several new imports and modify the return type of `create_pending_request` to include a match code as a fourth element in the tuple, along with adjusting the call site accordingly.

I'm also adding a helper function to resolve login hints to local DIDs — it checks if the hint is already a DID, otherwise normalizes it as a handle by stripping prefixes and validating the structure before looking it up in the database. Then I'm writing a dispatch helper that sends push notifications for login approvals, starting with an early return if the notification sender isn't available, then resolving the login hint to get the user's DID.

Writing dispatch helper... I'm working through the ordering problem here. If we push first and then fail to record the match code, the push goes out but the number isn't enforced—that's safe since approval still needs the device key. But if we set the row first and the push fails, we shouldn't return the code, which means the page won't display it, yet approval requires it. The real issue is that the match code needs to be displayed on the page whenever it's set on the row, regardless of whether the push succeeds.

For the enqueue-then-set approach, the risk window is tiny—between the notify returning and actually setting the flag, the wallet could theoretically approve without the number, but the push hasn't even reached APNs yet. For set-then-push, we'd want to only require matching when a push actually goes out, which means we need to know if any registrations with push handles exist before committing to the requirement. We could pre-check registrations to see if there are any with push handles, which gives us the fan-out condition without sealing failures.

Going with enqueue first, then set—if the set fails due to a DB error or race, we log a warning and return None. The page won't show a number, but the push tells the user to enter one anyway, creating a minor UX mismatch in an unlikely failure scenario. The wallet won't ask for the number since matchRequired is false, so the user can still approve. Also auditing PushDispatched after the set succeeds as a best-effort measure.

Now I'm checking the security angle—`create_pending_request` runs before render, and the GET handler isn't authenticated, so the login_hint is attacker-controllable. Anyone could type in a victim's handle at the login page.

This is exactly MFA fatigue. The mitigations are number matching (mandatory in this PR) plus rate limiting per client and IP, matching GitHub and Microsoft's approach. I'll note this in a comment and then write the edits.

file.content:
---
name: worktree-cargo-fmt-vendor-exclude
description: "cargo fmt --all (and thus just fmt-check / ci-pds step 1) fails in nested .claude/worktrees — vendored plugin crates resolve their workspace to the MAIN checkout, whose exclude paths don't match"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: reference
  originSessionId: dc1c745d-1c67-4801-bb36-e9007d43ea69
---

`cargo fmt --all` fails in any worktree under `.claude/worktrees/<name>/` with:

```
current package believes it's in a workspace when it's not:
current:   <worktree>/apps/identity-wallet/vendor/tauri-plugin-auth-session/Cargo.toml
workspace: /Users/jacob.zweifel/workspace/malpercio-dev/ezpds/Cargo.toml
```

**Why:** the vendored Tauri plugins (`apps/*/vendor/*`) are `workspace.exclude`d by
*relative* path and have no `[workspace]` table of their own. cargo-fmt's metadata walk
for a path-dep climbs past the worktree root and matches the MAIN checkout's Cargo.toml,
whose `exclude = ["apps/identity-wallet/vendor/..."]` doesn't match the nested
`.claude/worktrees/<name>/apps/...` path → hard error. Only affects `cargo fmt --all`
(and `just fmt-check`, the first `ci-pds` dependency); clippy/test/metadata run fine.

**Workaround:** run the pinned rustfmt binary directly on the files you touched:

```
~/.rustup/toolchains/1.96.0-aarch64-apple-darwin/bin/rustfmt --check --edition 2021 <files...>
```

then run the remaining `ci-pds` steps individually (lock-check, bruno-check, font-check,
cap-check, ios-paths-check, swift-rs-check, ios-template-check, clippy --all-targets,
test, audit, deny). CI itself (flat checkout) is unaffected. Related: [[worktree-cargo-via-main-devenv]].

Also: minimal env for cargo in a worktree without its own devenv —
`PATH=<main>/.devenv/profile/bin`, `LIBSQLITE3_SYS_USE_PKG_CONFIG=1`,
`PKG_CONFIG_PATH=<main>/.devenv/profile/lib/pkgconfig` (without the pkg-config path,
sqlx links macOS system sqlite and fails on `_sqlite3_load_extension`).

content.thinking:
I'm tracing through how my custom decoder handles different data types — when `data` is a string instead of an object, the container call returns nil, so the fields stay nil and everything decodes successfully. Same thing happens with numeric values like 7. The `decodeIfPresent` method catches type mismatches with try-catch, turning them into nil values, which keeps the decoding from failing even when the types don't match what I expect.

Now I'm realizing the flatMap chain with `decodeIfPresent` is creating an Optional of Optional situation, but the nil-coalescing operator flattens it back down to a single Optional, so it compiles fine. I should verify this actually works by running a typecheck on the Swift files — I can use the compiler to parse and typecheck the NotificationService code without needing to build the whole app.

1	# Shared iOS Swift sources
2	
3	Last verified: 2026-07-27
4	
5	## Purpose
6	
7	Swift that belongs to the iOS apps but to neither app's Rust crate. Today that is exactly one
8	thing: the wallet's **Notification Service Extension**, which unseals encrypted push
9	notifications on arrival.
10	
11	It sits at the repo root rather than under `apps/identity-wallet/` for the same reason
12	`scripts/ios/` does — the XcodeGen template that compiles it is shared by both apps, so its
13	inputs are shared too. The operator console will grow an extension from these same sources when it
14	adopts notifications.
15	
16	## Contracts
17	
18	### `NotificationService/` — the extension (`{{app.name}}_NSE`)
19	
20	**Exposes:** `NotificationService`, a `UNNotificationServiceExtension` subclass iOS
21	instantiates via `NSExtensionPrincipalClass` when a push carries `mutable-content: 1`.
22	
23	**Guarantees:**
24	- A payload that opens under HPKE Auth mode renders as content. **Everything else renders as
25	  the explicit unverified notice** — never a guess, never a partial render, never the relay's
26	  placeholder passed through as though it were news. This is the extension's single rule, and
27	  it holds on the timeout path too (`serviceExtensionTimeWillExpire`).
28	- The sealed `ezpds` block is stripped from the delivered notification, so ciphertext never
29	  reaches the app's delivered-notification list.
30	- Every failure leaves a breadcrumb in the shared Keychain, best effort. A Keychain that will
31	  not take a diagnostic never costs the user the notice itself.
32	
33	**Expects:**
34	- `keychain-access-groups` listing `$(AppIdentifierPrefix)org.obsign.shared` **first**
35	  (`apps/identity-wallet/src-tauri/Entitlements.NSE.plist`). Nothing here names an access group
36	  in a query — naming one would mean discovering `AppIdentifierPrefix` at runtime, on the one
37	  code path that must work on a locked screen — so the entitlement's *order* is the mechanism.
38	- The wallet having registered: `notification-key-priv` and `notification-sender-keys`, both
39	  under `kSecAttrAccessibleAfterFirstUnlock`, written by `notifications.rs`.
40	- iOS 17. `HPKE.Recipient`'s auth-mode initializer does not exist before it.
41	
42	| File | What it holds |
43	|---|---|
44	| `NotificationService.swift` | The `UNNotificationServiceExtension` shell, plus `NotifyResolver` — the pure failure ladder every branch of which is a banner someone reads |
45	| `NotifyCrypto.swift` | CryptoKit `HPKE.Recipient` in auth mode, suite/`info`/`aad` pinned to `crates/crypto/src/hpke.rs` |
46	| `NotifyEnvelope.swift` | Envelope + payload parsing, base64url, `did:key` → SEC1, base58 |
47	| `NotifyKeychain.swift` | The shared-Keychain reads, and the pin document's shape |
48	| `NotifyBreadcrumbs.swift` | The bounded failure log the app surfaces in Settings |
49	
50	### `NotificationServiceTests/` — the logic-test bundle (`{{app.name}}_NSETests`)
51	
52	Compiled with the extension's sources rather than linking them: an app extension has no
53	testable module to import, since there is no `TEST_HOST` an extension can be loaded into.
54	
55	`NotifyFixtureTests` is the **cross-implementation check** — it opens
56	`crates/crypto/tests/fixtures/notify/hpke-notify-v1.json` (sealed by Rust's `hpke` crate) with
57	CryptoKit. RFC 9180's appendix carries no vector for this suite, so nothing else proves the two
58	agree on the pinned suite, the `info` string, the empty `aad`, and the key encodings. The
59	fixture is referenced **in place** by the template — there is no copy here to drift.
60	
61	## Dependencies
62	
63	System frameworks only: CryptoKit, Foundation, Security, UserNotifications. Deliberately no
64	Swift package dependency — a package in the extension is a second supply chain in the one
65	process that runs on a locked screen.
66	
67	## Key Decisions
68	
69	- **Swift, not a second Rust staticlib.** Decryption is ~200 lines of CryptoKit; a second
70	  staticlib would double the iOS build's slowest step for it.
71	- **Breadcrumbs go to the shared Keychain, not an app-group container.** The keychain group is
72	  already entitled and needs no Apple Developer portal work; an app group would be a second new
73	  entitlement on both bundles. The cost is that a push arriving before the first unlock after a
74	  reboot leaves no breadcrumb — the one failure that repairs itself, and the least worth
75	  recording.
76	- **The extension is gated to the wallet's bundle id** in `scripts/ios/project.yml`. An app
77	  extension is a separate bundle needing its own App ID, profile, and signing secret; rendering
78	  one for admin-companion would cost a second set of those for an extension that cannot decrypt
79	  anything until the console has a shared keychain group and registered notification keys of its own.
80	
81	## Invariants
82	
83	- The Keychain service name, account names, and both JSON document shapes in
84	  `NotifyKeychain.swift` / `NotifyBreadcrumbs.swift` are **copies** of constants in
85	  `apps/identity-wallet/src-tauri/src/{keychain,notifications}.rs`. Two separate bundles can
86	  only agree by both spelling the same strings; a rename on one side is silent on the other.
87	- `PRODUCT_MODULE_NAME` is pinned to `NotificationService` in the template. It is half of
88	  `NSExtensionPrincipalClass`, so a drift leaves iOS unable to instantiate the extension — a
89	  failure indistinguishable from a push that never arrived. `just ios-check` greps the pbxproj
90	  for it.
91	- The failure `reason` vocabulary (`NotifyFailureReason`) is shared with the app's
92	  `NotificationFailure.reason` and the frontend's `NotificationFailureReason`. Both readers
93	  tolerate an unrecognized value on purpose: the extension versions independently, and the entry
94	  a strict reader would drop is the one the user is asking about. A new case still needs wording
95	  in `apps/identity-wallet/src/lib/notification-health.ts`.
96	- CI gates, in order of what they can catch:
97	  - `just _nse-typecheck` (macOS, part of `just ios-pr-check`) — `swiftc -typecheck` of the
98	    extension's sources, then of the test bundle exactly as the template composes it, against
99	    the real iOS SDK at the deployment target both apps declare. No simulator, no signing, no
100	    generated Xcode project. This is the only thing that compiles this Swift before a release
101	    archive would.
102	  - `just ios-template-check` (Linux) — target present, gated to the wallet, embedded,
103	    principal class and module name, entitlements order and least privilege, sources exist.
104	  - `just ios-check` (macOS) — the same structural facts in the generated pbxproj.
105	  Nothing *runs* the tests in CI: `ios-pr-check` performs no `xcodebuild`, so the fixture
106	  cross-check is a local `xcodebuild test -scheme <app>_NSETests` (or `⌘U` on that scheme).

# Shared iOS Swift sources

Last verified: 2026-07-27

## Purpose

Swift that belongs to the iOS apps but to neither app's Rust crate. Today that is exactly one
thing: the wallet's **Notification Service Extension**, which unseals encrypted push
notifications on arrival.

It sits at the repo root rather than under `apps/identity-wallet/` for the same reason
`scripts/ios/` does — the XcodeGen template that compiles it is shared by both apps, so its
inputs are shared too. The operator console will grow an extension from these same sources when it
adopts notifications.

## Contracts

### `NotificationService/` — the extension (`{{app.name}}_NSE`)

**Exposes:** `NotificationService`, a `UNNotificationServiceExtension` subclass iOS
instantiates via `NSExtensionPrincipalClass` when a push carries `mutable-content: 1`.

**Guarantees:**
- A payload that opens under HPKE Auth mode renders as content. **Everything else renders as
  the explicit unverified notice** — never a guess, never a partial render, never the relay's
  placeholder passed through as though it were news. This is the extension's single rule, and
  it holds on the timeout path too (`serviceExtensionTimeWillExpire`).
- The sealed `ezpds` block is stripped from the delivered notification, so ciphertext never
  reaches the app's delivered-notification list.
- Every failure leaves a breadcrumb in the shared Keychain, best effort. A Keychain that will
  not take a diagnostic never costs the user the notice itself.

**Expects:**
- `keychain-access-groups` listing `$(AppIdentifierPrefix)org.obsign.shared` **first**
  (`apps/identity-wallet/src-tauri/Entitlements.NSE.plist`). Nothing here names an access group
  in a query — naming one would mean discovering `AppIdentifierPrefix` at runtime, on the one
  code path that must work on a locked screen — so the entitlement's *order* is the mechanism.
- The wallet having registered: `notification-key-priv` and `notification-sender-keys`, both
  under `kSecAttrAccessibleAfterFirstUnlock`, written by `notifications.rs`.
- iOS 17. `HPKE.Recipient`'s auth-mode initializer does not exist before it.

| File | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `NotificationService.swift` | The `UNNotificationServiceExtension` shell, plus `NotifyResolver` — the pure failure ladder every branch of which is a banner someone reads |
| `NotifyCrypto.swift` | CryptoKit `HPKE.Recipient` in auth mode, suite/`info`/`aad` pinned to `crates/crypto/src/hpke.rs` |
| `NotifyEnvelope.swift` | Envelope + payload parsing, base64url, `did:key` → SEC1, base58 |
| `NotifyKeychain.swift` | The shared-Keychain reads, and the pin document's shape |
| `NotifyBreadcrumbs.swift` | The bounded failure log the app surfaces in Settings |

### `NotificationServiceTests/` — the logic-test bundle (`{{app.name}}_NSETests`)

Compiled with the extension's sources rather than linking them: an app extension has no
testable module to import, since there is no `TEST_HOST` an extension can be loaded into.

`NotifyFixtureTests` is the **cross-implementation check** — it opens
`crates/crypto/tests/fixtures/notify/hpke-notify-v1.json` (sealed by Rust's `hpke` crate) with
CryptoKit. RFC 9180's appendix carries no vector for this suite, so nothing else proves the two
agree on the pinned suite, the `info` string, the empty `aad`, and the key encodings. The
fixture is referenced **in place** by the template — there is no copy here to drift.

## Dependencies

System frameworks only: CryptoKit, Foundation, Security, UserNotifications. Deliberately no
Swift package dependency — a package in the extension is a second supply chain in the one
process that runs on a locked screen.

## Key Decisions

- **Swift, not a second Rust staticlib.** Decryption is ~200 lines of CryptoKit; a second
  staticlib would double the iOS build's slowest step for it.
- **Breadcrumbs go to the shared Keychain, not an app-group container.** The keychain group is
  already entitled and needs no Apple Developer portal work; an app group would be a second new
  entitlement on both bundles. The cost is that a push arriving before the first unlock after a
  reboot leaves no breadcrumb — the one failure that repairs itself, and the least worth
  recording.
- **The extension is gated to the wallet's bundle id** in `scripts/ios/project.yml`. An app
  extension is a separate bundle needing its own App ID, profile, and signing secret; rendering
  one for admin-companion would cost a second set of those for an extension that cannot decrypt
  anything until the console has a shared keychain group and registered notification keys of its own.

## Invariants

- The Keychain service name, account names, and both JSON document shapes in
  `NotifyKeychain.swift` / `NotifyBreadcrumbs.swift` are **copies** of constants in
  `apps/identity-wallet/src-tauri/src/{keychain,notifications}.rs`. Two separate bundles can
  only agree by both spelling the same strings; a rename on one side is silent on the other.
- `PRODUCT_MODULE_NAME` is pinned to `NotificationService` in the template. It is half of
  `NSExtensionPrincipalClass`, so a drift leaves iOS unable to instantiate the extension — a
  failure indistinguishable from a push that never arrived. `just ios-check` greps the pbxproj
  for it.
- The failure `reason` vocabulary (`NotifyFailureReason`) is shared with the app's
  `NotificationFailure.reason` and the frontend's `NotificationFailureReason`. Both readers
  tolerate an unrecognized value on purpose: the extension versions independently, and the entry
  a strict reader would drop is the one the user is asking about. A new case still needs wording
  in `apps/identity-wallet/src/lib/notification-health.ts`.
- CI gates, in order of what they can catch:
  - `just _nse-typecheck` (macOS, part of `just ios-pr-check`) — `swiftc -typecheck` of the
    extension's sources, then of the test bundle exactly as the template composes it, against
    the real iOS SDK at the deployment target both apps declare. No simulator, no signing, no
    generated Xcode project. This is the only thing that compiles this Swift before a release
    archive would.
  - `just ios-template-check` (Linux) — target present, gated to the wallet, embedded,
    principal class and module name, entitlements order and least privilege, sources exist.

## Purpose

I'm working through how NSDictionary's generic type parameters work in Objective-C interop—NSDictionary defaults to `<AnyObject, AnyObject>` when untyped, and when calling `objectForKey`, the key parameter expects `AnyObject`, so an `NSString` reference gets automatically coerced upward through the deref and AsRef trait chain that connects NSString to NSObject to AnyObject.

For downcasting, I can use `Retained<AnyObject>::downcast::<NSDictionary>()` which returns a Result, and then extract string values by downcasting the returned objects to NSString and converting them to Rust strings.

I need to enable the "NSDictionary" feature for objc2-foundation, and for objc2-user-notifications I'll need "UNNotificationResponse", "UNNotification", "UNNotificationRequest", and "UNNotificationContent" features. For block invocation, I'll call the completion block using `unsafe { (*completion).call(()) }`.

/**
 * Sign and submit a decision for a previewed authorization. `grantedScope` is the space-joined
 * scope set the wallet chose (empty for a denial). Gate this behind `authenticateBiometric()` — it
 * is the authorization boundary that signs the consent envelope with the identity's device key.
 *
 * `matchCode` is the two-digit number the user read off the sign-in page — required to approve
 * when the preview said `matchRequired` (a wrong number is `MATCH_CODE_MISMATCH` and the request
 * stays pending for a retype); never needed to deny.
 */
export const confirmOAuthConsent = (
  did: string,
  requestId: string,
  clientId: string,
  decision: 'approve' | 'deny',
  grantedScope: string,
  matchCode?: string
): Promise<ConsentDecision> =>
  invoke('confirm_oauth_consent', {
    did,
    requestId,
    clientId,
    decision,
    grantedScope,
    matchCode: matchCode ?? null,
  });

I see that grep found the ticket reference in a comment within the Svelte component, though the linter only checks Rust files and the agents document. Now I'm setting up the component state with a reactive variable to track the consent request ID, then implementing a handler that processes notification routes and filters for login-approval events.

The handler checks whether we're on an interruptible onboarding step, fetches the list of identities, resolves which DID to use (preferring the one specified in the route if it exists, or defaulting to the only identity if there's just one), then updates the component state and navigates to the consent approval screen. I'm also noting that I should verify whether the `goTo` function clears any alarm takeover state that might interfere.

Now I'm thinking through the sequencing in `onMount` — the notification route handler needs to run after the home step is assigned and after `checkAndLand` completes, but the timing matters because if a consent route exists, it should take priority over any alarm takeover. The `landOnAlarm` function already guards against navigating away from the consent approval screen, so as long as the drain runs right after the identities block, the consent route should win the race.

The cleanest approach is to reverse the order: drain the notification route first before triggering the alarm takeover, since the drain is fast anyway. I'd make `handleNotificationRoute` return a boolean indicating whether it actually routed somewhere, then only call `checkAndLand` if nothing was routed — that way the consent prompt gets priority and we skip the alarm takeover for this launch.

For the warm event listener, I'm setting up a notification route event handler that reads from the slot and processes pending routes, maintaining single-consumption semantics. The consent step needs to track which request ID it's handling, clearing it when the user navigates away or completes the flow — I should wire this up in the back/done handlers and also when signing in through the identity screen.

I need to import the notification route utilities and then make these edits.

content.content:
Obsign now reads the encrypted notifications your Custos instance sends. Until now your phone could receive one but not open it, so every notification arrived as a placeholder; a small extension bundled with the app now unseals each one the moment it arrives — on the lock screen, without waking the app, and without the relay in the middle or Apple ever seeing the text. What you read is what your server wrote.

When a notification *cannot* be opened, Obsign says so plainly rather than showing you something that looks genuine. iOS does not let an app silently discard a notification, so anything that fails to unseal — a relay sending noise, a message signed with a key your phone has not seen, or one arriving before you have unlocked your phone since restarting it — appears as an explicit "Couldn't verify a notification from your Custos instance". It is never dressed up as real content, which is what stops whoever carries your notifications from being able to put words in your server's mouth.

Because that notice on its own cannot tell you *which* of those happened, Settings gains a Notifications section that can. It counts the recent failures and names the likely cause in plain language — and, where there is something to do, says what: a key mismatch is usually fixed by opening one of your identities, since Obsign refreshes the keys on every contact with your server, while a run of unrecognisable notifications points at the relay rather than at anything of yours being at risk. Once you have dealt with it, you can clear the record so the next real report is not lost in an old one.

Until now your phone could receive one but not open it, so every notification arrived as a placeholder; a small extension bundled with the app now unseals each one the moment it arrives — on the lock screen, without waking the app, and without the relay in the middle or Apple ever seeing the text. What you read is what your server wrote.

When a notification *cannot* be opened, Obsign says so plainly rather than showing you something that looks genuine. iOS does not let an app silently discard a notification, so anything that fails to unseal — a relay sending noise, a message signed with a key your phone has not seen, or one arriving before you have unlocked your phone since restarting it — appears as an explicit "Couldn't verify a notification from your Custos instance". It is never dressed up as real content, which is what stops whoever carries your notifications from being able to put words in your server's mouth.

Because that notice on its own cannot tell you *which* of those happened, Settings gains a Notifications section that can. It counts the recent failures and names the likely cause in plain language — and, where there is something to do, says what: a key mismatch is usually fixed by opening one of your identities, since Obsign refreshes the keys on every contact with your server, while a run of unrecognisable notifications points at the relay rather than at anything of yours being at risk. Once you have dealt with it, you can clear the record so the next real report is not lost in an old one.

input.content:
Signing in to an app can now come to you. When a sign-in page knows which account it is for, your Custos instance sends a sealed push to Obsign; tapping it opens the approval screen directly on that request — no code to type, no QR to scan. The push travels the same encrypted path as every Obsign notification: the relay carries an opaque sealed payload and an opaque delivery handle, so neither it nor Apple ever learns that a login is happening, for whom, or from where. And Obsign only acts on a tapped notification it could cryptographically verify came from your instance.

Because a prompt that finds *you* is exactly where tap-fatigue attacks live, approval on this channel demands one extra proof: the sign-in page shows a two-digit number, and Obsign requires you to type it before Face ID. If someone else started that login, you are not looking at their screen, so there is nothing you can type — a blind "Approve" is impossible, and your server enforces the number, not just the app. A wrong number never kills the request; denying it (which needs no number) does, and is exactly the right answer to a prompt you did not start.

If the push never arrives — notifications off, relay down, a new phone — nothing is lost: the same sign-in page still shows the typed code and the QR, and either one opens the same request in Obsign, where the number is still asked for and still on the page in front of you.

input.old_string:
- **Phase C — push + number matching.** After the notification relay (MM-311) lands:
  `login-approval` notification type, deep-link approve/deny, number-match UX.
input.new_string:
- **Phase C — push + number matching.** After the notification relay (MM-311) lands:
  `login-approval` notification type, deep-link approve/deny, number-match UX.
  **Landed (2026-07-29):** when the consent page's `login_hint` names a hosted account
  (resolved with **local lookups only** — the hint is attacker-suppliable on an
  unauthenticated surface, so no outbound handle resolution), Custos seals a
  `login-approval` payload to the account's registered devices over the existing
  notification pipeline (`notifications::notify_device`, which now reports the enqueued
  count) and latches a two-digit `match_code` + `push_dispatched_at` onto the pending row
  (V060, single-use guarded UPDATE). The sealed payload carries display text plus
  `data: {requestId, did, clientName, origin}` — **deliberately not the relay design's
  `code` field**: the number is the proof the approver can see the login surface, so
  handing it to the wallet would defeat the channel binding. The consent page displays the
  number; the wallet preview reports `matchRequired`; and `/oauth/authorize/approve`
  refuses an approval whose `matchCode` doesn't match (403, request left pending for a
  retype — checked server-side, outside the signed envelope, after the signature/authority
  checks). A denial never requires the number (declining must not be harder than
  approving). Delivery: the NSE forwards a verified payload's routing identifiers as the
  `ezpdsRoute` userInfo block; the wallet's new tap handler (`apns.rs` +
  `notification_routes.rs`) parks the route and the frontend deep-links into
  `OAuthConsentApprovalScreen` on the `request_id` (re-fetching everything displayed
  server-side, the QR-path discipline). Push failure degrades to the Phase A/B channels on
  the same request, with the number still displayed and still enforced.
  **Number-format decision:** type-the-number (GitHub style), two digits — typing removes
  the guess-tap surface entirely, where select-from-three leaves a 1-in-3 blind tap.
